title: GST 111 (COOU) | Chapter Two: Note-Taking and Note-Making — Okafor, Ifeyinwa A.
subject: GST 111

questions.question: Note taking is best described as a process of:
options: Recording every single word the lecturer utters in the class
Copying a colleague's notebook after the lecture has ended
Memorising all that the lecturer says during the lecture
Reading through several textbooks before an examination
questions.explanation: Note taking is a process of writing down pieces of information in a systematic way.

questions.question: It is impossible for one to retain everything he hears because of the:
options: Poor quality of lecture delivery in many universities
Absence of modern recording devices in classrooms
Fast pace at which many lecturers speak
questions.explanation: The chapter states that one cannot retain everything because of the limited nature of our memories.

questions.question: Note taking makes one to concentrate fully on what one is:
questions.explanation: Note taking makes one concentrate fully on what one is listening to or reading.

questions.question: Good notes should show the organisation of the text and the:
options: Author's personal biography and family background
Total number of pages in the original textbook
Publisher's name and the year of publication
Market price of the textbook in bookshops
questions.explanation: Good notes should show the organisation of the text and the relationship between the ideas.

questions.question: A direct relationship exists between what happens in lectures and what comes up in the:
questions.explanation: There is a direct relationship between what happens in lectures and what comes up in the exam.

questions.question: Which of these is the first procedure to taking good notes?
options: Review your notes from the previous lecture
Read background material before the class
Position yourself at the back of the class
Ask the lecturer questions during the lecture
questions.explanation: The first procedure listed is gathering your note-taking material before the start of any lecture.

questions.question: Before a lecture, a student using a laptop should ensure that it is:
questions.explanation: If using a laptop, make sure it is fully charged or that you can sit near a power outlet.

questions.question: Students who wear glasses should have them during lectures in case the lecturer writes on the:
questions.explanation: Glasses are needed in case the lecturer writes down important information on a black or white board.

questions.question: Reviewing notes from the last lecture before a new class helps a student to:
options: Understand the lecturer's accent much better
Make new friends among his classmates
Avoid taking any notes during lectures
Pick up where he left off
Score high marks in the examination automatically
questions.explanation: Reviewing previous notes brings you fully up to speed and ready to pick up where you left off.

questions.question: According to the chapter, if you fail to prepare, you:
questions.explanation: The chapter states: if you fail to prepare, you prepare to fail.

questions.question: The key to good note-taking is:
options: Recording the lecture on a tape
questions.explanation: The key to good note-taking is understanding, not mindlessly writing every word.

questions.question: Many people make the mistake of mindlessly taking down:
questions.explanation: Many people make the mistake of mindlessly taking down every word without comprehending.

questions.question: Research shows that note takers retain information better when they take notes:
questions.explanation: Research shows note takers retain information better when they take notes by hand.

questions.question: People typing on a laptop tend to transcribe every word without:
questions.explanation: People typing on a laptop tend to transcribe every word without understanding the meaning.

questions.question: In a lecture, there will probably be three or four main points linked by:
questions.explanation: There will probably be three or four main points linked by a common theme.

questions.question: Illustrations, examples and student interactions in a lecture are described as:
options: The main points of the lecture
The key ideas of the whole topic
The summary of the whole lecture
The central theme of the lecture
The rest of the class work
questions.explanation: The rest of the class work may well be illustrations, examples, exercises and student interactions.

questions.question: A new lecture should be started on:
questions.explanation: A new lecture will be started on a fresh page with the details of the lecture written out.

questions.question: When starting a new lecture, you should write the lecturer's name, the date and the:
questions.explanation: You write the details of the lecture: the name of the lecturer, the date and the topic.

questions.question: Major divisions of a lecture are best observed from the:
questions.explanation: Note the major divisions of a lecture from the opening statements of the speaker.

questions.question: Large space should be left in the margin for:
options: Recording the date of the lecture
questions.explanation: Leave large space in the margin for comments and cross referencing.

questions.question: A note taker should distinguish between major points and:
questions.explanation: Try to distinguish between major points and supporting details.

questions.question: Digressions in a lecture include jokes, extended explanations and:
questions.explanation: Digressions include jokes, extended explanations and intrusions, as distinct from examples and definitions.

questions.question: Examples, illustrations, justifications and definitions are described as:
options: Cue words used by the speaker
questions.explanation: Examples, illustrations, justifications and definitions are supporting details, not digressions.

questions.question: Which of these pairs are described as cue words?
options: Days of the week and months
questions.explanation: Cue words include therefore, however, in addition, on the contrary and at last.

questions.question: A note taker is advised to write content words in accordance with the speaker's:
questions.explanation: Write content words only in accordance with the speaker's emphasis.

questions.question: Notes should be written using intelligible phrases rather than:
questions.explanation: Notes should use intelligible phrases rather than full sentences.

questions.question: Branching, diagrams and charts are used in notes to:
questions.explanation: Branching, diagrams and charts are used to represent ideas where practicable.

questions.question: Once a lecture is over, a student should return to his notes to:
questions.explanation: After the lecture, go back to your notes as soon as possible to fill in the gaps you created.

questions.question: Areas of notes that are still unclear should be marked for clarification from textbooks or:
questions.explanation: Unclear areas are marked for further clarification from textbooks or your lecturer.

questions.question: Note making is described as being right at the heart of:
questions.explanation: Note making is right at the heart of academic study.

questions.question: Students make notes when they attend lectures or seminars and when they:
options: Listen to the radio at home
questions.explanation: Students make notes when they attend lectures or seminars and read to support essay and report writing.

questions.question: Note making is a process of reviewing, connecting and:
questions.explanation: Note making is a process of reviewing, connecting and synthesising ideas from lecturers or reading.

questions.question: Making notes helps you to stay active and engaged during lectures, reading and:
questions.explanation: Making notes helps you stay active and engaged during lectures, reading and revision.

questions.question: Making notes helps you to be selective and identify:
questions.explanation: Making notes helps you be selective and identify key ideas.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the three stages of note-making?
questions.explanation: The three stages of note-making are before, during and after.

questions.question: During the note-making stage, a student should note down main ideas and:
questions.explanation: During the stage, note down main ideas and key words, and find techniques that work for you.

questions.question: In the 'after' stage of note-making, a student should reflect, review and then:
questions.explanation: After the lecture you reflect, review and then organise your notes.

questions.question: One major difference between note-making in lectures and when reading is the lack of:
questions.explanation: The big difference is the lack of control the student has over the process, because lectures happen in real time.

questions.question: When reading, unlike in lectures, you can easily stop and:
questions.explanation: When reading you can easily stop and read something again if you need to.

questions.question: The risks in note-making from reading relate to notes that are too detailed and notes that are too:
questions.explanation: The risks relate to note-making that is too detailed and note-making that is too brief.

questions.question: Being too brief in note-making carries the risk of failing to record:
questions.explanation: If too brief, you fail to record crucial material and have to go back to the source.

questions.question: Being too comprehensive in note-making may result in the reader running out of:
questions.explanation: Being too comprehensive means reading takes far too long, you end up with masses of notes and run out of time.

questions.question: The key to successful note making is being:
questions.explanation: The risk can be managed by being selective, for that is the key to successful note making.

questions.question: One level of selectivity in note making is deciding what to read and what not to read; the other is deciding:
questions.explanation: The two levels are deciding what to read and what not to read, and deciding which specific materials to make notes on.

questions.question: Good notes should contain source information such as title, author and:
questions.explanation: All good notes should contain source information such as title, author and date.

questions.question: Triggers that make notes more memorable include colour and:
questions.explanation: Triggers to make your notes more memorable include colour or drawings.

questions.question: The Cornell note-taking method helps to organise class notes into easily digestible:
questions.explanation: The Cornell method helps organise class notes into easily digestible summaries.

questions.question: In the Cornell method, the paper is divided into:
questions.explanation: The paper is divided into two columns: a cue word column and a notes column.

questions.question: In the Cornell method, the first column is used to enter:
questions.explanation: The first column is used to enter key or cue words while the second is the notes column.

questions.question: In the Cornell method, each main idea is recapitulated in complete sentences at the bottom of the:
questions.explanation: Recapitulate each main idea using complete sentences at the bottom of the key word column.
